title: Digital receptors & film processing
blurb: Film, phosphor plates and digital sensors: how each records the image, how to handle and process them, and what can go wrong.
question: Your practice uses phosphor plates, but a locum dentist asks you to take a film from the old stock and process it by hand. Afterwards you notice a used phosphor plate has been left on the worktop under the surgery light for twenty minutes before scanning. What do you need to know about each receptor to handle this safely?

teach.body: The receptor is whatever records the X-rays after they pass through the patient. There are three kinds in dental practice. Conventional film uses a chemical emulsion that must be developed in a darkroom. Phosphor plates (PSP, photostimulable phosphor) store the image until a laser scanner reads it. Solid-state digital sensors (CCD or CMOS) turn X-rays straight into an electronic signal, so the image appears on screen within seconds. Most UK practices now use digital, but film is still taught and still found.

teach.caption: Digital receptors avoid wet processing, allow image adjustment and secure storage and sharing, and generally need less exposure than film.

teach.body: A phosphor plate holds a hidden (latent) image until it is scanned. Bright light gradually erases it, so plates left exposed to light before scanning give a pale, grainy or partly erased image. Scan promptly and keep plates in their light-tight packet. After scanning, the reader or a light box erases the plate ready for reuse. Plates crack if over-bent, scratch if handled roughly or bitten, and can be damaged by liquid getting in, so always use a fresh barrier envelope and clean them exactly as the manufacturer says.

head: Layer
Job
rows: Keeps out saliva and light; raised dot for orientation
Emulsion of silver halide crystals records the image
Absorbs scatter from behind; faces away from the tube
teach.caption: If a film is placed back to front, the beam passes through the lead foil first, giving a pale image with the foil's pattern on it.

steps.label: Develop
steps.sub: Exposed crystals turn to black metallic silver

steps.label: Rinse
steps.sub: Water removes developer and stops development

steps.label: Fix
steps.sub: Removes unexposed crystals; makes the image permanent

steps.label: Wash
steps.sub: Removes all chemicals so the film won't discolour

teach.caption: Done by hand in a darkroom under a safelight, or in an automatic processor. Times and temperatures follow the manufacturer's instructions.

teach.body: Developer and fixer are hazardous substances covered by COSHH, so wear gloves and eye protection and follow the safety data sheets. Used processing chemicals and lead foils are hazardous waste and are collected by a licensed contractor, never poured down the sink or put in general waste. Processors need regular cleaning and fresh chemicals. For digital systems, receptors are inspected for damage and checked for even (uniform) images as part of the practice's quality assurance, and every check is recorded.

teach.text: Developer acts on EXPOSED crystals (they go black); fixer removes UNEXPOSED crystals (those areas stay clear and look white). Order: develop → rinse → fix → wash → dry.

items: Three receptors: film (chemical), phosphor plate (indirect digital), sensor CCD/CMOS (direct digital).
Phosphor plates: scan promptly, keep from light, avoid bending and scratching, erase before reuse.
Film packet: wrapper, black paper, film, lead foil; raised dot for orientation.
Film processing: develop, rinse, fix, wash, dry. Chemicals and lead foil are hazardous waste.

summary: You can now compare film, phosphor plates and digital sensors, handle phosphor plates without damaging or erasing the image, name the layers of a film packet, list the film processing stages in order, and dispose of processing waste safely.

A.q: Which receptor produces an image on the computer screen within seconds, with no scanning step?
A.why: Direct digital sensors (CCD or CMOS) convert X-rays straight into an electronic image almost instantly.

whyNot.0: Phosphor plates must be scanned in a reader before the image appears.
whyNot.1: Film must be chemically processed first.
whyNot.3: An occlusal film is still film and needs processing.

A.q: A used phosphor plate is left under the surgery light for a long time before scanning. What is the likely result?
A.why: Light gradually erases the latent image stored on a phosphor plate, leaving a pale or grainy image.

whyNot.0: Light exposure removes image information, so it won't get darker or clearer.
whyNot.2: Sharpness can only get worse, not better.
whyNot.3: Phosphor plates are sensitive to light, so the image does change.

A.q: What is the correct order for manual film processing?
A.why: The film is developed, rinsed to stop development, fixed to make it permanent, washed and then dried.

whyNot.0: Fixing first would remove the crystals before an image could be developed.
whyNot.1: Rinsing comes before fixing, and washing must happen before drying.
whyNot.2: The film must be developed before anything else.

B.q: What is the purpose of the lead foil inside a film packet?
options: To absorb scatter from behind the film
To make the image appear faster
To keep saliva and light out of the packet
To show which way up to mount it
B.why: The lead foil absorbs scattered radiation from behind the film, which would otherwise fog the image.

whyNot.1: Lead has no effect on processing speed.
whyNot.2: The outer wrapper and black paper keep saliva and light out, not the foil.
whyNot.3: Orientation is shown by the raised dot, not the foil.

B.q: What does the fixer do during film processing?
B.why: Fixer removes the unexposed silver halide crystals and hardens the emulsion, making the image permanent.

whyNot.0: Turning exposed crystals black is the developer's job.
whyNot.1: Drying is a separate stage; fixer doesn't warm the film.
whyNot.3: Fixer hardens the emulsion rather than softening it.

B.q: How should used fixer solution be disposed of?
options: Diluted and poured down the sink
Mixed with the developer and binned
B.why: Used processing chemicals are hazardous waste and must be collected by a licensed waste contractor.

whyNot.0: Processing chemicals must never go down the drain.
whyNot.1: Clinical waste bags are for infectious waste, not liquid chemicals.
whyNot.2: Mixing chemicals is unsafe, and they still can't go in general waste.

C.q: Which statement about phosphor plates is correct?
options: They are rigid and attached by a USB cable
They are erased and reused after scanning
C.why: Phosphor plates store a latent image, are scanned by a laser reader and then erased with light so they can be reused.

whyNot.0: Rigid, wired receptors describe solid-state sensors.
whyNot.3: Plates need scanning; instant images come from direct sensors.

C.q: A film is placed in the mouth back to front. How will the image look?
C.why: The beam passes through the lead foil first, which absorbs much of it, leaving a pale image marked with the foil pattern.

whyNot.1: The foil reduces exposure, so the image is pale, not dark.
whyNot.2: Reversing the packet always affects the image.
whyNot.3: A completely black film suggests light exposure, not reversal.

C.q: Which is a disadvantage of a solid-state digital sensor compared with a phosphor plate?
options: It must be erased with bright light after use
It is rigid and bulkier in the mouth
C.why: Sensors are thicker, rigid and often wired, which some patients find uncomfortable to hold in the mouth.

whyNot.0: No digital system needs a darkroom.
whyNot.1: Erasing with light applies to phosphor plates.
whyNot.3: Sensors have no chemical processing at all.

reteach.title: Three kinds of camera
reteach.question: Think of an old roll-film camera, a camera you have to plug into a printer, and a phone camera. How do they match the three receptors?

blocks.body: Film is the old roll-film camera: you must develop it in chemicals in the dark before you can see anything, and you can't reuse it. A phosphor plate is like a memory card you have to put into a reader: the picture is stored invisibly, light can wipe it, and once read you can clear it and use it again. A digital sensor is the phone camera: the picture is on the screen almost straight away.

blocks.text: Light is the enemy of both film AND phosphor plates before processing: it fogs film and erases plates.

explain.body: Direct digital sensors (CCD or CMOS) send the image straight to the computer within seconds. They're reusable but rigid, thicker, often wired and expensive, and can crack if dropped or bitten.

test.q: Which receptor type uses a CCD or CMOS chip?
test.why: CCD and CMOS are the electronic chips inside direct digital sensors.

whyNot.0: Phosphor plates use a phosphor coating read by a laser.
whyNot.1: Film uses a silver halide emulsion.
whyNot.3: Cassette film is still chemical film.

explain.body: Plates store a latent image, are scanned by a laser reader, then erased for reuse. Keep them away from light before scanning, don't bend or scratch them, and always use a barrier envelope.

test.q: Why should a phosphor plate never be bent sharply to fit the mouth?
test.why: Over-bending cracks the phosphor layer, leaving permanent white line artefacts on future images.

whyNot.0: Light, not bending, erases the image.
whyNot.2: Bending doesn't change the dose delivered.
whyNot.3: The reader still works, but the damaged plate gives poor images.

explain.body: From the tube side: plastic wrapper with a raised dot, black paper, the film, then lead foil at the back to absorb scatter. Reversing the packet gives a pale image with the foil pattern.

test.q: What does the raised dot on a film packet help with?
test.why: The raised dot shows the side facing the tube, so the film can be mounted the right way round.

whyNot.1: Scatter is absorbed by the lead foil.
whyNot.2: The plastic wrapper keeps saliva out.
whyNot.3: The dot has no effect on processing time.

explain.body: Develop (exposed crystals go black), rinse, fix (unexposed crystals removed, image made permanent), wash, dry. Chemicals are COSHH-hazardous and collected as hazardous waste.

test.q: A film turns brown months after processing. Which stage was most likely inadequate?
test.why: Inadequate washing leaves chemicals on the film, which turns it brown over time.

whyNot.0: Developer problems show straight away as a pale or dark image.
whyNot.2: Poor drying causes marks or sticking, not later browning.
whyNot.3: Exposure faults show as a pale or dark image at once.
